title: Resilient Schema Negotiation + Non-blocking Tool-Call Acceptance Criteria
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Define acceptance criteria and test scenarios for making structured output and tool/function-calling resilient in the face of partial emissions, schema drift, tool latency, and intermittent errors. Focus is on: 1) graceful partial responses that remain machine-parseable; 2) non-blocking tool call semantics so caller receives usable output while long-running tool work proceeds; 3) schema negotiation & soft-fallback rules; 4) clear observability and recovery signals for operators.
background: Customers are integrating Redwood inference into workflows that rely on typed JSON outputs and automatic tool invocation. We continue to surface incidents where models return malformed fragments under streaming or when downstream tools are slow/unavailable. Existing acceptance docs emphasize deterministic envelopes, but operational needs require: non-blocking behavior, richer error taxonomy for partial outputs, and explicit schema reconciliation paths to avoid total failure of calling applications.
goals: Ensure streamed structured responses are always recoverable by consumer parsers: minimal envelope guarantees even on partial emission or mid-stream failures.
Define non-blocking tool-call behavior so API returns usable result markers without waiting for long-running tool completion (with optional async callback or follow-up event).
Specify schema negotiation and backward-compatible reconciliation rules for runtime mismatches between model-emitted types and consumer expectations.
Define observability events and metrics required to diagnose partial-schema regressions and tool-call degradations.
scope: Acceptance criteria and test plan for hosted API streaming & non-streaming endpoints.
Behavior spec for tool/function invocation handshake, including timeouts and fallback routing (e.g., route to text-only variant).
Telemetry/trace requirements (events emitted on schema mismatch, tool call start/complete/fail, partial-envelopes).
Consumer-facing error codes and recommended client-side retry/backoff approaches.
out_of_scope: Implementation details for on-prem/private deployments (handled separately).
Model fine-tuning or generator-level training changes to enforce schema (we rely on runtime enforcement and validation).
Full SDK changes for every language—we will specify canonical behavior and add SDK tasks as follow-ups.
success_metrics: Reduction in production incidents where downstream services reject model output due to malformed JSON by 80% within first rollout month.
>= 99% of streamed sessions deliver an initial valid envelope within 200ms of first byte emitted.
Tool-call availability: when primary tool is unavailable, 100% of calls return a documented fallback envelope rather than timing out without a consumable payload.
Increase in signal-rich telemetry for schema mismatches (new event emitted) to 100% coverage for test harnesses.
acceptance_criteria:
Envelope baseline: Every response that claims a structured payload MUST begin with a single-line ASCII envelope header: 'RI-STRUCT-v1 <trace_id> <schema_version>
'. Consumer libraries will depend on this header to decide parser flow. Even if body streaming fails, header must be emitted before any tool-call handshake (if model is capable).

Partial emission validity: If the model emits a fragment that is syntactically incomplete, the runtime shall append a "partial" recovery object in the final frame when termination occurs. Example final frame: {"_redwood_partial": true, "_expected_schema": "task-v2/order", "fields_received": ["order_id", "items"]}. This object MUST be valid JSON and parsable on its own.

Non-blocking tool call: For tool invocations flagged as 'long-running' by policy, the API MUST return an immediate structured acknowledgement envelope with a stable call_id and current schema shape, and optionally a short result summary. Example: {"status": "in_progress", "call_id": "abc123", "schema": "payment-quote-v1"}. The server will emit a follow-up asynchronous event (webhook or subscription) when final output is available.

Synchronous fallback: If a long-running tool is configured to be blocking and exceeds the knobbed timeout (default 5s), the runtime MUST return a documented 'deferred' envelope as above rather than failing the entire request. The original request context (trace_id, call_id) must be preserved for follow-ups.

Schema negotiation: When model-emitted field types mismatch consumer-requested types (e.g., string vs object), the runtime shall attempt the following reconcilers in order: 1) coercion (stringified JSON -> parsed object if looks like JSON), 2) wrap scalar in canonical field e.g., {"value": <scalar>}, 3) mark reconciliation in diagnostic fields on the envelope and emit a 'schema_mismatch' telemetry event. Acceptance requires automated tests for all three reconcilers.

Error taxonomy: The API must surface machine-readable error codes in the envelope final frame. Minimum codes: SCHEMA_MISMATCH, PARTIAL_EMIT, TOOL_UNAVAILABLE, TOOL_TIMEOUT, TOOL_ERROR, PARSE_FAILURE. Each code must include human_message and remedial_action keys. Example: {"error_code": "TOOL_TIMEOUT", "human_message": "Payment provider timed out, see call_id for retries.", "remedial_action": "retry_async"}.

Streaming termination codes: Streaming sessions must end with an explicit terminal marker frame containing: terminal_code (OK | PARTIAL | FAILED), call_id (if any), summary_stats (tokens_emitted, elapsed_ms), and a signed checksum of preceding structured frames to help clients detect truncation. Tests must simulate mid-stream TCP drop and confirm clients can detect truncation via checksum.

Idempotency & replay: Tool-calls issued via the runtime must be idempotent when a call_id is provided by the client. If the client does not provide a call_id, the runtime will generate one and annotate the outbound tool invocation. Replays must be detectable by tool backends via call_id header. Acceptance requires integration test with a mock tool service verifying call deduplication.

Backpressure and flow control: When consumer is slow or applies small window, the runtime must prioritize emitting header and minimal envelope before continuing to full body streaming. Runtime should support pausing model generation without losing KV cache state and resume when consumer window expands. Acceptance requires a test harness that artificially throttles the client connection and verifies header arrival within SLO.

Observability: For every structured session the runtime must emit these trace events: session.start, envelope.header_emitted, tool.call.started (per tool), tool.call.completed, envelope.terminal, schema.mismatch. Each event must include trace_id, call_id (if applicable), model_id, schema_version, and a short diagnostic string. Acceptance requires dashboards to show 99th-percentile time between header_emitted and tool.call.completed.
test_plan: Unit tests for envelope generation: generate header-only responses and verify adherence to ASCII header format and header parsing library (positive and negative cases).

Streaming truncation simulation: open a streaming session, simulate abrupt connection drop at several offsets (early/late) and assert that client-side parser either consumes partial object as valid partial object or raises explicit truncation error detected via checksum.

Non-blocking tool-call flow: instrument mock long-running tool (sleep 10s). Confirm API returns immediate in_progress envelope and that webhook callback contains final structured payload with same call_id. Validate dedup semantics by repeating same call_id twice and confirming single effective tool execution.

Schema reconcilers: create test cases where model emits stringified JSON, scalar where object expected, or nested type mismatch. Verify runtime applies coercion/wrap/reconciliation and emits schema_mismatch event when reconciliation is applied.

Tool outage fallback: simulate tool returning 503. Confirm runtime emits TOOL_UNAVAILABLE envelope and returns documented fallback payload (e.g., summary or best-effort). Verify SLO: fallback emitted < 300ms after tool error observed.
Telemetry end-to-end: enable debug tracing and run a mixed workload; assert that each session emits required trace events and that dashboards ingest them (mock ingestion acceptable for acceptance).
Performance SLO test: under 90th percentile production-like load, header_emitted must be within 200ms for 99% of requests and tool-call deferred envelope < 500ms.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): Enable header + partial-envelope behavior for 5% of traffic on hosted API with verbose debug telemetry. Monitor metrics for schema_mismatch events and parsing errors.
Phase 2 (broader): Expand to 50% with non-blocking tool-call flag enabled for long-running tool config. Run integration tests with key customers who depend on async tool flows.
Phase 3 (GA): Default enabled for all structured-output endpoints. Publish SDK guidance and sample client parsers for graceful degradation patterns.
Communication: provide migration guide & changelog, and schedule office hours with top 10 customers to walk through behavior and Q/A.
implementation_notes: Runtime change required: emit ASCII envelope header before invoking model I/O for structured routes to guarantee consumer detection.
Add terminal frame serializer that can compute a lightweight streaming checksum (e.g., CRC32) across frames. Must be compact to avoid large overhead on small responses.
Tool-caller middleware should accept an optional call_id header from client; when missing, generate stable UUID and propagate to outbound tool HTTP call as 'X-RI-Call-Id'.
Telemetry: augment tracing library to include schema_version and reconciliation_flag in spans so search queries can filter schema-related regressions.
open_questions: Should the ASCII header be negotiated to v2 with explicit capability flags (e.g., supports_deferred_callbacks) or keep single v1 and extend via diagnostic fields?
What is the default server-side timeout for long-running tool calls before we switch to deferred mode? (proposed default 5s, configurable per project).
For on-prem/private installs, do we keep the same webhook-based callback pattern or provide a polling API only? This affects security review.
Is signed checksum sufficient for truncation detection or do we need per-frame signed sequence numbers to detect reorder/dup?
